name: Centro
etymology_summary: Self-explanatory: the historic centre of Madrid, the original core around the Puerta del Sol and Plaza Mayor.

name: Arganzuela
etymology_summary: From 'Arganduela' meaning 'Pequena Arganda' (little Arganda). Settlers from Arganda del Rey established themselves on the south bank of the Manzanares river.

name: Retiro
etymology_summary: From the Palacio del Buen Retiro (1633), built by Felipe IV as a royal retreat. The word 'retiro' means retreat/rest. Origin traces to the San Jeronimo el Real monastery where monarchs retired during Lent and mourning periods.

name: Salamanca
etymology_summary: Named after Jose de Salamanca y Mayol (1811-1883), Marquis of Salamanca, politician, financier, and real estate developer who planned and built the neighbourhood in the mid-19th century.

name: Chamartin
etymology_summary: Former independent municipality annexed in 1948. From Basque origin, per Menendez Pidal (1951). The documented medieval form 'Echamartin' (1247) contains the Castilian evolution of Basque 'aita' (father/chief), appearing in documents as 'ecta/echa'. Thus: Echa-Martin > Chamartin = 'the estate of chief Martin'. Same pattern as Chaherrero (Avila) and Robledo de Chavela.
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae (toponhisp.org/es/toponimia-de-las-zonas-central-sur-e-insular-atlantica/toponimo/chamartin); Menendez Pidal 1951; documented form 'Echamartin' 1247; CVC Rinconete; Garcia Sanchez 2010

name: Tetuan
etymology_summary: Named 'Tetuan de las Victorias' after Spanish troops returning from victory at Tetouan (Morocco) in the African War of 1860. The soldiers camped in this area upon their return, and the settlement that grew around it took the name.

name: Chamberi
etymology_summary: Disputed etymology. The most probable link is via Queen Barbara de Braganza, who founded the Royal Salesas Convent (c.1748) with nuns from Chambery/Annecy in Savoy; the toponym first appears on Chalmandrier's 1761 map. Alternative: Luisa Gabriela de Saboya (wife of Felipe V). The Napoleonic regiment theory is refuted by the 1761 map predating Napoleon. Other theories: French regiment during War of Independence; Celtic origin.
source: Pedro de Repide; Chalmandrier map 1761; Secretos de Madrid; Caridad Arias 2004; Chamberi30dias; Ayuntamiento de Madrid 'Historia de Chamberi'

name: Fuencarral-El Pardo
etymology_summary: Compound name. Fuencarral: from 'Fuente Carral' -- a spring (fuente) where carts (carros) stopped and animals drank on the old road to Alcobendas. The stopping place for carts was called a 'carra'. El Pardo: from the brownish/dark ('pardo') colour of the landscape of the royal hunting estate.
source: El Rincon de Mayrit; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuencarral; Historias Matritenses; Vena Madrid

name: Moncloa-Aravaca
etymology_summary: Compound name. Moncloa: from the Palacio de la Moncloa, possibly from 'Mons Clovis' (Latin). Now the official residence of the Prime Minister. Aravaca: Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004) argues for Celtic origin, with the root *ara- meaning 'water'. First documented 1427; appears in Alfonso VIII's 1222 fuero.

name: Latina
etymology_summary: Named after Beatriz Galindo 'La Latina' (1465-1534), a humanist scholar who was Latin tutor and advisor to Queen Isabel la Catolica. She founded the Hospital de la Latina in this area.

name: Carabanchel
etymology_summary: Former independent municipalities (Alto and Bajo) annexed in 1948. The most accepted etymology traces it to the pre-Roman/Indo-European root *kar-/*karav- meaning 'stone' (per Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953), describing 'stony ground'. Menendez Pidal links it to Garabandal (Cantabria) as a variant. The earliest documented form is 'Caravangiel/Caravanchel' (1 January 1181, original parchment in Archivo de la Catedral de Toledo); 'Carauanchiel' appears in 1264. Alternatives: Arabic 'carab' (cultivable land, per Oliver Asin); 'garbanzal' (chickpea field); Illyrian anthroponym Caravantius with diminutive Carabancilius (per Caridad Arias 2004).
source: Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004: dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=3012173); Oliver Asin; Archivo Catedral de Toledo (1181 doc)

name: Usera
etymology_summary: Named after Colonel Marcelo Usera, who married the daughter of 'Tio Sordillo', a farmer whose lands he proposed to develop into housing plots (1925-1930).

name: Puente de Vallecas
etymology_summary: 'Vallecas' from 'Valle de Cas' (oak valley), documented as 'Balecas' in the 1202 Fuero de Madrid. 'Puente' (bridge) refers to a bridge over the Abroigal stream that connected the area to Madrid proper.

name: Moratalaz
etymology_summary: Hybrid pre-Arabic/Arabic toponym per Teres Sadaba (CSIC 1986): 'Morat' (pre-Arabic/Visigothic: elevated place/height) + 'Alfaz' (Arabic: sown/cultivated field) = 'cultivated field on a height'. First documented as 'Morat Alfaz' in 1206 in a property deed benefiting the Order of Calatrava. Madrid-specific first mention: 1425. Alternative: from vulgar Latin *Muratella* (from *murus*: wall).

name: Ciudad Lineal
etymology_summary: Named after Arturo Soria y Mata's (1844-1920) revolutionary 'Ciudad Lineal' (linear city) urban planning concept, conceived 1882/1886 and built 1892-1911. A narrow city stretching along a single transportation axis, with the boulevard Calle de Arturo Soria as its spine.

name: Hortaleza
etymology_summary: Former independent village annexed to Madrid in 1950. First documented 1361. Disputed etymology: (1) Latin 'hortus' (garden/orchard) -- most commonly cited but weakened by Felipe II's 1579 Relaciones noting main crops were cereals, not vegetables; (2) Latin 'Orta Lucis' (sunrise) -- proposed by Vicente Muzas in La Ciudad Lineal no. 323 (1907), supported by the historical spelling 'Ortaleza' without H until mid-19th century; (3) Corruption of 'fortaleza' (fortress) -- no archaeological remains found.
source: Relaciones topograficas Felipe II 1579; Muzas 1907 (La Ciudad Lineal no. 323); periodicohortaleza.org/la-fabula-del-nombre-de-hortaleza; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hortaleza_(municipio)

name: Villaverde
etymology_summary: 'Villa verde' = green village/town, from Latin 'villa viridis'. A descriptive name referring to the verdant landscape of this former independent municipality south of Madrid. Annexed by Madrid in 1954.

name: Villa de Vallecas
etymology_summary: 'Vallecas' etymology debated: from Latin 'vallis' + Arab personal name 'Kas', or from 'Vallis Egas'. 'Villa' denotes its former status as an independent municipality. First documented in 1202 in the Fuero de Madrid as 'Balecas'. Independent until annexed by Madrid in 1950.

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: From 'Vico Alvaro' = Alvaro's village/settlement. A pre-medieval personal name attached to the Latin 'vicus' (village). Former independent municipality annexed in 1951. Famous for the 'Vicalvarada' or Pronunciamiento de Vicalvaro (1854), a military uprising led by General O'Donnell.

name: San Blas-Canillejas
etymology_summary: Compound name. San Blas: patron saint (Saint Blaise, 4th-century Armenian bishop and martyr) of the original parish church. Canillejas: ancient municipality documented from the 13th century, annexed in 1949. Canillejas served as an agricultural settlement for over six centuries.

name: Barajas
etymology_summary: Former independent municipality annexed in 1949. Etymology debated: (1) Bar Axa theory: Philip II's 1575 Relaciones topograficas record 'en tiempo que los moros fue senor de este pueblo un moro llamado Baraja hijo de una mora llamada Aja'. Covarrubias (Tesoro 1611) supports this. (2) Latin *varalia* (fence of crossbars) per Nieto Ballester (1997). (3) Latin *uaralia* (quarrel/litigation) per Gutierre Tibon. (4) Pre-Roman toponym per Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007).
source: Philip II Relaciones topograficas 1575; Covarrubias, Tesoro de la lengua 1611; Nieto Ballester 1997; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007); cvc.cervantes.es/foros/leer_asunto1.asp?vCodigo=45869
